name: WebRTC ICE host candidates (mDNS)
plain: WebRTC used to expose the device's local network IP; browsers now hide it behind a random .local name.
meaning: RTCPeerConnection gathers ICE host candidates. Since 2019 and 2020 Chrome and Firefox replace private IPs with mDNS .local names, but granting getUserMedia (camera or microphone) restores real addresses.

fields.name: host candidate
fields.precision: hidden by default in modern browsers

limits.headline: Can try to find your device's home network address, but browsers now hide it
limits.user_action: You join a video call or visit a site that sets up a call connection
can: Start a call connection that lists your device's network addresses
See a random .local name in place of your real home network address in Chrome and Firefox
See your real home network address if you have also allowed camera or microphone
cannot: See your real home network address by default in Chrome and Firefox since 2019 and 2020
Set this up without a site script running
See other devices on your network from this alone
Be sure to bypass a VPN, since modern browsers mask the address
limits.differs: Chrome and Firefox hide the address by default. Safari asks differently and also shows a masked name unless camera or microphone is allowed.

story.what_it_is: Video call tech used to show your device's home network address. Browsers now hide it behind a random name.

marketing.name: mDNS ICE candidates
marketing.pitch: Browsers swap your local address for a random .local name, so calls still connect but the real address stays private.

story.for_you: On a video call or a multiplayer game you notice nothing. Behind the scenes your browser offers a random name instead of your home network address. Calls still work.
story.for_makers: Makers need these candidate addresses to link two devices directly, which cuts server cost and delay. Hiding the real address stops sites from quietly reading it, but direct links on the same network still work.

use_cases.example: Two coworkers on the same office Wi-Fi join a Google Meet call. Their browsers swap random local names and connect straight to each other, which keeps audio crisp.
A browser party game uses peer to peer data channels. Players on the same Wi-Fi link directly through hidden local names, so moves arrive with low delay.
A cloud gaming stream in a browser sets up a direct media path from the game server to the player. Hidden local names stop the page leaking the player's network layout.
A web chat app starts a voice room. Friends on one network connect with each other without sending audio through the company's servers.
A tracking script used to read local addresses to tell devices apart. With hidden names it gets a random value that changes, so that trick stops working.
A telehealth site lets a doctor and patient talk. It keeps the call direct when possible and avoids storing home addresses in logs.
A virtual classroom opens small group rooms. Students in the same school building connect over the local network, so lessons run smoothly.

technical_bounds: Still leaks IPv6 addresses in some cases

value.abuse: VPN bypass detection and local IP leak, LAN inventory
